opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what kind of problem you're actually trying to solve. If the goal is to incrementally push existing benchmarks, then yes, a team of very established people is probably the most efficient choice. They know the playbook and they execute well. But if you believe, as I do, that some of the most important questions in AI are still open, like how models should truly understand the visual world or how to build real world models rather than just better text predictors, then the playbook itself might be the problem.

Established researchers carry a lot of priors. That's their strength, but it can also be a burden. When you've succeeded with a certain paradigm for ten years, it's very hard to walk away from it, psychologically and professionally. Young people often don't have that baggage. They're willing to question things that everyone else treats as settled, and sometimes they're naive in a very productive way. Many of the ideas that ended up mattering in our field came from people who didn't yet know "that's not how it's done."

The mission-driven part matters just as much, maybe more. Research at the frontier is a long grind. Most of the time, things don't work. If someone is here mainly for the title, the compensation, or the résumé line, the first few months of failure will wear them down, or they'll drift toward safer, more publishable directions. Someone who genuinely cares about the question will stay with it, and that persistence is often what separates a real breakthrough from a nice paper.

There's also a cultural reason. A small team of hungry, curious people who trust each other can move incredibly fast. Communication is direct, ego is low, and people are willing to do the unglamorous work, like cleaning data or building infrastructure, because they see it as part of the mission. With a room full of stars, you sometimes spend a lot of energy just negotiating who leads what.

That doesn't mean experience doesn't matter. Mentorship is really important, and I see part of my role as providing taste, judgment, and protection so young people can take big swings. But I'd rather bet on people whose best work is ahead of them, and help them get there, than assemble people whose best work might already be behind them. In a period where the field is changing this fast, I think that's actually the less risky bet.

r001.rationale: The response says a small, trusting team can move fast and that a room full of stars may spend energy negotiating roles, but it does not clearly reject assembling established researchers in the hope that productive chemistry will emerge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what you're actually trying to build. If you assemble a team of very established researchers, you get people who already have their own agenda, their own reputation to protect, their own sense of what the "right" problem is. That's not bad, but it's a very different thing from a group of people who are all pulling in the same direction.

When I think about the moments in my own career that mattered most, they were almost never when I was the most senior person in the room. They were when I was young, somewhat naive, and working with a few people who genuinely believed in a problem and didn't care that much about whether it was fashionable. The ResNeXt work, the early self-supervised learning work at FAIR, ConvNeXt later on. In every case, the energy came from people who were willing to spend a year on something that might not pan out, and who weren't constantly calculating how it would look on their CV.

Mission-driven young people have a few things going for them. First, they're not yet anchored. They haven't decided what the field "is," so they're more willing to ask questions that an established researcher would consider settled or embarrassing. A lot of real progress in vision came from exactly those questions. Second, they have time horizons that match the problem. If you believe something is going to take three or five years, you need people who are okay living inside that uncertainty. Senior people often can't afford that. They have students, grants, commitments. Third, and this is maybe underrated, they teach me things. The best students I've had have changed how I think about the field, not the other way around.

I also think there's a cultural point. If I hire five famous people, I'm basically running a conference. Everyone presents, everyone is polite, nobody really builds together. If I hire five people who are hungry and aligned on a mission, the lab becomes a single organism. People share code, share failures, argue about ideas late at night. That kind of density is where the surprising stuff comes out.

Of course, this isn't a rule against experience. Some of the most important collaborators I've had were extremely senior, like Kaiming or Ross. But those relationships worked because they were also mission-driven, not because of their titles. So the real criterion isn't age. It's whether someone is in it for the problem. It just happens that, statistically, you find more of those people early in their careers, before the incentives of the field have had a chance to reshape them.

r001.rationale: The response argues that assembling famous, highly established researchers is unlikely to produce shared building: they bring separate agendas, and the group would act like a conference rather than collaborate closely.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key is ownership. When you’re trying to build something uncertain, you need people who care enough about the mission to ask, “What needs to happen, and how can I make it happen?” They’re not just looking for a well-defined problem that fits their expertise.

Young researchers can be especially exciting because they’re still forming their ideas. They’re willing to learn, challenge assumptions, and grow with the team. If you give them real responsibility, they can surprise you.

That doesn’t mean established researchers aren’t valuable. Experience matters enormously. But a collection of impressive individual résumés doesn’t automatically become a great team. I’d prioritize people who share a purpose, trust each other, and are willing to do the work the mission requires. Age is secondary to that.

r001.rationale: The response says a collection of impressive résumés does not automatically make a great team, and prioritizes shared purpose and trust. This rejects relying on established researchers’ credentials alone to produce team cohesion.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the most important thing is whether someone really believes in the problem we’re trying to solve. If you’re doing research where the direction is uncertain, you need people who will take ownership, question assumptions, and keep going when an experiment fails. You can’t get that just by putting impressive résumés together.

Young researchers often haven’t settled into one particular way of doing things. They’re willing to learn and try something that looks a little unreasonable. If you give them real responsibility, they can grow with the project and help define its direction.

That doesn’t mean experience isn’t valuable. It absolutely is. But I wouldn’t use reputation as a substitute for motivation. I’d rather build around people who care deeply about the mission and want to figure things out together.

r001.rationale: The response says impressive résumés alone cannot ensure ownership and motivation, but it does not clearly reject assembling established researchers in the hope that productive team chemistry will emerge.
